## 1. What you'll build, and why

Phase 3 grows the *language*. We start with `struct` — Swift's fundamental building block and your
first **value type**. A struct bundles named **stored properties** into one aggregate, with a
**memberwise initializer** Swift gives you for free. Its defining behaviour is **value semantics**:
assigning a struct **copies** it, so changing the copy never affects the original. `Int`, `Bool`,
`Double`, `Array`, `String`, `Dictionary` — almost everything in Swift is a value type. This is the
single biggest design difference from most languages, and you're about to make it real.

- **You implement:** the new syntax through the compiler: lexing, parsing, struct registration and
  type checking, then member **read** and **write** in SILGen and the struct instructions in IRGen.
  The AST/type/SIL contracts and the repetitive construction plumbing are given.
- **Outcome:** struct programs **run and match swiftc**, value semantics included — the oracle
  test compiles a 16-program corpus with both compilers and compares every byte of output.

## 2. Concepts in depth

### A struct is an aggregate

`struct Point { var x: Int; var y: Int }` declares a type whose values are two `Int`s laid out
side by side — an **aggregate**. In LLVM that's a named type, `%Point = type { i64, i64 }`; a
`Point` variable is an `alloc_stack` slot big enough to hold both fields. Sema records each struct's
**layout** (its fields, in order) in a registry that SILGen and IRGen consult to turn a field *name*
into an *index*.

### Value semantics — the whole point

@fig-value-semantics follows two statements, starting from a `Point` `p` holding `x = 1`,
`y = 2`: first `var q = p` (left), then `q.x = 99` (right).

![Value semantics: `var q = p` copies the whole aggregate into q's own slot, so `q.x = 99` changes only q — p still reads 1.](figs/value_semantics.png){#fig-value-semantics}

`p` and `q` are two separate stack slots, and `var q = p` copies the contents of one into the
other. Here is the program behind the figure:

```swift
struct Point {
  var x: Int
  var y: Int
}
var p = Point(x: 1, y: 2)
var q = p
q.x = 99
print(p.x)
print(q.x)
```

and the SIL it lowers to:

```
sil @main() -> $() {
bb0:
  %0 = integer_literal $Int, 1
  %1 = integer_literal $Int, 2
  %2 = struct (%0, %1) $Point        // Point(x: 1, y: 2)
  %3 = alloc_stack $Point  // p      // p's slot
  store %2 to %3                     // var p = ...
  %5 = load %3 $Point                // var q = p: read all of p...
  %6 = alloc_stack $Point  // q      // q's slot
  store %5 to %6                     // ...and write it into q's slot
  %8 = integer_literal $Int, 99
  %9 = struct_element_addr %6, #0    // q.x = 99: field 0's address, in q's slot
  store %8 to %9
  %11 = load %3 $Point               // print(p.x)
  %12 = struct_extract %11, #0 $Int
  %13 = apply @print(%12)
  %14 = load %6 $Point               // print(q.x)
  %15 = struct_extract %14, #0 $Int
  %16 = apply @print(%15)
  return
}
```

`var q = p` is a `load` of the whole `Point` out of p's slot (`%3`) and a `store` into q's (`%6`).
`q.x = 99` writes to an address computed from q's slot, so it cannot reach p's: the program prints
`1` for `p.x` and `99` for `q.x`. Nothing extra was needed to get this: two slots, and copying
between them, *is* value semantics.

A `class` (Phase 6) is the opposite. Its variable holds a pointer to one object on the heap, so
`var q = p` copies the pointer, and after `q.x = 99` reading `p.x` gives `99` too. Whether a type is
a value or a reference comes down to what copying it copies: the contents, or a pointer to them.

Returning a struct from a function follows the same rule. `ret %Point %value` hands back the value
itself, not a pointer into the callee's stack frame, which is gone once the function returns; the
caller gets its own copy. How that value physically travels — in registers, or through a buffer
the caller provides — is set by the platform's calling convention, and does not change that.

### Reading vs. writing a field — value vs. address

Reading a field and writing one are lowered differently. Both appear in the SIL of the program
above:

- **Reading `p.x`** works on a copy. `load` the whole `Point` out of p's slot, then take field 0 of
  that value with `struct_extract` (LLVM `extractvalue`):

  ```
  %11 = load %3 $Point               // a copy of all of p
  %12 = struct_extract %11, #0 $Int  // its field 0, x
  ```

  Any struct value can be read this way, not only a variable: a function result, or a
  `Point(x: 1, y: 2)` built on the spot.

- **Writing `q.x = 99`** cannot work on a copy: changing a field of a copy changes the copy, and
  `q` stays as it was. It has to change the bytes in q's own slot. So it computes the *address* of
  field 0 inside that slot with `struct_element_addr` (LLVM `getelementptr`), and `store`s there:

  ```
  %9 = struct_element_addr %6, #0    // where q.x lives, inside q's slot %6
  store %8 to %9                     // write 99 there; q.y is untouched
  ```

  (A copy *could* be made to work: load all of `q`, build a new `Point` with field 0 replaced,
  store the whole thing back. That is three steps, and it rewrites fields that did not change; the
  address goes straight to the one field.)

A write therefore needs a variable to write into, since only a variable has a slot. swiftc rejects
`f().x = 3` ("cannot assign to property: 'f' returns immutable value"), and in our subset the
parser only accepts a variable name before `.x =`. And because the address is computed from q's
slot, writing `q.x` cannot reach `p`'s.

Writing a field of a `let` is rejected by a separate rule: Sema refuses it before any SIL exists,
with swiftc's message, "cannot assign to property: 'p' is a 'let' constant".

Both halves need one more thing, and it is this concept's contribution to the typed tree: **which**
field. The source writes a *name*; what it means is a *position* in the layout, and the position is
what both SIL instructions take. So the checker resolves it, once, and the tree records it —
`Tast.Field (base, index, name)` for the read, an index on `Tast.Set_member` for the write. The name
survives only for printing.

```swift
struct P {
  var x: Int
  var y: Int
}
let p = P(x: 1, y: 2)
print(p.y)
```

Saved as `p.swift`, the last line of its typed tree is the `print`:

```bash
$ ./lab.exe --emit-tast p.swift | tail -1
(print (field (local p : P) #1 y : Int) : ())
```

`#1` is the answer SILGen consumes. It performs no lookup of its own, which also means it cannot
disagree with the layout the program was type-checked against — the two can no longer drift apart.

### The memberwise initializer

An *initializer* is the code that creates a value of a type; `Point(x: 1, y: 2)` calls one. Swift
lets a struct declare its own, as `init`. When a struct declares none, Swift writes one for it,
with one parameter per stored property — per `var` field — in declaration order. For `Point`,
that is as if you had written:

```swift
struct Point {
  var x: Int
  var y: Int
  init(x: Int, y: Int) {   // written by Swift, not by you
    self.x = x
    self.y = y
  }
}
```

Hence the name *memberwise*: one argument per member. Its parameters are named after the fields,
and in Swift a parameter's name is also the label the call must write, so the call is
`Point(x: 1, y: 2)`: labels required, in field order. Sema checks the labels and the types, and a
missing or wrong label is an error, as in swiftc. In our subset the struct cannot declare an
`init` of its own (that is a v1 feature), so this memberwise one is the only way to make a
`Point`.

A label only says which field a value goes into, and once Sema has checked `x:` against field 0
and `y:` against field 1, the *order* of the values says the same thing. So, like the field name
in `p.y` above, the labels stop at the checker. The two trees for `let p = Point(x: 1, y: 2)`:

```
(let p (Point x:1 y:2))
(let p (init Point (int_lit 1 : Int) (int_lit 2 : Int) : Point))
```

The first is the AST, as written, labels included. The second is the typed tree: its `init`
(`Tast.Struct_init`) holds only the two values, in field order, so SILGen builds the `Point`
without reading a label.

The initializer lowers to a **`struct`** instruction that builds the aggregate value from its
fields. LLVM has no single struct-construction instruction: IRGen starts with `undef`, an
aggregate whose fields have no specified values, then each `insertvalue` produces a new aggregate
with one field filled. After every field has been inserted, the final aggregate is the complete
`Point`.

Here is the whole path in one small program. To illustrate both value semantics and field
selection, it copies a `Point`, then writes all three fields and reads fields with different
indices and LLVM types. The writes change only `q`:

```swift
struct Point {
  var x: Int
  var y: Int
  var visible: Bool
}
var p = Point(x: 3, y: 4, visible: true)
var q = p
q.x = 9
q.y = 8
q.visible = false
print(p.x)
print(q.x)
print(q.y)
print(q.visible)
```

It prints `3`, `9`, `8`, then `false`. The three writes select fields `#0`, `#1`, and
`#2`; the last field also shows that an aggregate can mix an `Int` with a differently
represented `Bool`. The corresponding SIL makes construction, copying, writing, and reading
separate operations:

```text
struct Point { x: Int; y: Int; visible: Bool }

sil @main() -> $() {
bb0:
  %0 = integer_literal $Int, 3
  %1 = integer_literal $Int, 4
  %2 = integer_literal $Bool, true
  %3 = struct (%0, %1, %2) $Point
  %4 = alloc_stack $Point  // p
  store %3 to %4
  %6 = load %4 $Point
  %7 = alloc_stack $Point  // q
  store %6 to %7
  %9 = integer_literal $Int, 9
  %10 = struct_element_addr %7, #0
  store %9 to %10
  %12 = integer_literal $Int, 8
  %13 = struct_element_addr %7, #1
  store %12 to %13
  %15 = integer_literal $Bool, false
  %16 = struct_element_addr %7, #2
  store %15 to %16
  %18 = load %4 $Point
  %19 = struct_extract %18, #0 $Int
  %20 = apply @print(%19)
  %21 = load %7 $Point
  %22 = struct_extract %21, #0 $Int
  %23 = apply @print(%22)
  %24 = load %7 $Point
  %25 = struct_extract %24, #1 $Int
  %26 = apply @print(%25)
  %27 = load %7 $Point
  %28 = struct_extract %27, #2 $Bool
  %29 = apply @print(%28)
  return
}
```

IRGen translates that graph directly. `undef` supplies an aggregate with no initialized fields;
the two `insertvalue` instructions produce successively more complete `Point` values. Runtime
declarations are omitted here:

```llvm
%Point = type { i64, i64, i1 }

define i32 @main() {
bb0:
  %t0 = alloca %Point
  %t1 = alloca %Point
  %t2 = insertvalue %Point undef, i64 3, 0
  %t3 = insertvalue %Point %t2, i64 4, 1
  %t4 = insertvalue %Point %t3, i1 1, 2
  store %Point %t4, ptr %t0
  %t5 = load %Point, ptr %t0
  store %Point %t5, ptr %t1
  %t6 = getelementptr %Point, ptr %t1, i32 0, i32 0
  store i64 9, ptr %t6
  %t7 = getelementptr %Point, ptr %t1, i32 0, i32 1
  store i64 8, ptr %t7
  %t8 = getelementptr %Point, ptr %t1, i32 0, i32 2
  store i1 0, ptr %t8
  %t9 = load %Point, ptr %t0
  %t10 = extractvalue %Point %t9, 0
  call i32 (ptr, ...) @printf(ptr @.fmt_int, i64 %t10)
  %t11 = load %Point, ptr %t1
  %t12 = extractvalue %Point %t11, 0
  call i32 (ptr, ...) @printf(ptr @.fmt_int, i64 %t12)
  %t13 = load %Point, ptr %t1
  %t14 = extractvalue %Point %t13, 1
  call i32 (ptr, ...) @printf(ptr @.fmt_int, i64 %t14)
  %t15 = load %Point, ptr %t1
  %t16 = extractvalue %Point %t15, 2
  %t17 = select i1 %t16, ptr @.btrue, ptr @.bfalse
  call i32 (ptr, ...) @printf(ptr @.fmt_str, ptr %t17)
  ret i32 0
}
```

The aggregate `load` followed by an aggregate `store` is the copy from `p` into `q`.
The final index of each `getelementptr` selects `x`, `y`, or `visible`. These are field indices,
not byte offsets: LLVM derives the actual byte offset from `%Point = type { i64, i64, i1 }`,
including any alignment padding. The `extractvalue` indices select the same three fields from a
loaded aggregate.

There are two indices in `getelementptr %Point, ptr %t1, i32 0, i32 2`. The first `0` means
“stay at the `Point` addressed by `%t1`”; a `1` there would move to the next complete `Point`.
The second index selects field 2, `visible`. LLVM requires a struct-field index to be a constant
`i32`; it is a field identifier, unrelated to the field's own `i1` type. The first index is
allowed to use another integer width, but this IR generator consistently emits `i32`.

### The three new SIL instructions (swiftc's exact names)

| SIL | meaning | LLVM |
|---|---|---|
| `struct (%a, %b)` | build an aggregate from fields | `insertvalue` chain |
| `struct_extract %v, #i` | read field *i* from a struct **value** | `extractvalue` |
| `struct_element_addr %p, #i` | address of field *i* of a struct **address** | `getelementptr` |

swiftc emits these same instructions; the value/address split (`struct_extract` vs.
`struct_element_addr`) is straight from real SIL — read `swift/lib/SILGen/SILGenConstructor.cpp` for
the synthesized initializer and `swift/docs/SIL.rst` for the instructions.

### The subset you are growing into

**New lexemes.** Two punctuation marks and a keyword; the keyword table lives in `token.ml`
(`keyword_or_ident`), the punctuation in `lexer.ml`:

| spelling | token | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `struct` | `Token.Kw_struct` | a keyword, like `func` — it starts a top-level *item* |
| `.` | `Token.Dot` | shares the `'.'` arm with `..<`: peek for `.` `<` first, else it is a `Dot` |
| `;` | `Token.Newline` | Swift's statement separator; lexing it *as* a newline is what lets `struct P { var x: Int; var y: Int }` fit on one line |

No new operator, so the precedence table is concept 07's — member access is **postfix**, applied
after a primary is parsed and before any infix operator is considered, so it binds tighter than
everything.

**The grammar** — `<-- new` marks what this concept adds; everything else is concepts 05–09.
Notation is EBNF: `[ x ]` is *optional* (zero or one), `{ x }` is *repetition* (zero or more),
`|` separates alternatives, and quoted text is a terminal.

```
program     ::= [ nl ] [ item { nl item } ] [ nl ]
nl          ::= NEWLINE { NEWLINE }     # a run of blank lines is one separator
item        ::= struct_decl                                        <-- new
              | func_decl
              | statement
struct_decl ::= "struct" ident "{" [ nl ] [ field { nl field } ] [ nl ] "}"   <-- new
field       ::= ("var" | "let") ident ":" type                     <-- new
func_decl   ::= "func" ident "(" [ param { "," param } ] ")" [ "->" type ] block
param       ::= [ label ] ident ":" type
block       ::= "{" [ nl ] [ statement { nl statement } ] [ nl ] "}"

statement   ::= ("let" | "var") ident [ ":" type ] "=" expr
              | ident "=" expr
              | ident "." ident "=" expr                           <-- new (member write)
              | if-stmt                     
              | "while" expr block
              | "for" ident "in" expr "..<" expr block
              | "break" | "continue" | "return" [ expr ]
              | expr
if-stmt     ::= "if" expr block [ "else" ( block | if-stmt ) ]
block       ::= "{" [ nl ] [ statement { nl statement } ] [ nl ] "}"
type        ::= "Int" | "Double" | "Bool" | "String" | "Void"
              | ident                                              <-- new (a struct name)

expr        ::= or
or          ::= and { "||" and }                                     (bp 3)
and         ::= comparison { "&&" comparison }                       (bp 4)
comparison  ::= cast { ("==" | "!=" | "<" | "<=" | ">" | ">=") cast } (bp 5)
cast        ::= sum { "as" type }                                    (bp 7)
sum         ::= product { ("+" | "-") product }                      (bp 10)
product     ::= unary { ("*" | "/" | "%") unary }                    (bp 20)
unary       ::= "-" unary | postfix
postfix     ::= primary { "." ident }                              <-- new (member read)
primary     ::= int | float | string | "true" | "false" | ident
              | ident "(" [ arg { "," arg } ] ")"
              | "(" expr ")"
arg         ::= [ ident ":" ] expr                                 <-- new (argument labels)
```

Three things to notice. A `struct` declaration is an **item**, not a statement — like `func`, it is
legal only at top level, so `parse_program` gains one case: it already sends `Kw_func` to
`parse_function`, now sends `Kw_struct` to the struct parser, and everything else still goes to
`parse_statement`. The member *write* is a **statement production**, not an assignment to an
arbitrary expression: the parser commits to it on a four-token lookahead (`ident` `.` `ident` `=`),
which is why `l.b.x = 1` — two levels deep — is not in this subset. And a call argument may now
carry a **label**; the parser records it for every call, sema *checks* it only for a memberwise
initializer (a `func` still takes its arguments positionally, concept 07's simplification).

### The new AST contract

```ocaml
type expr =
  | (* earlier cases *)
  | Call of string * arg list * Token.span
  | Member of expr * string * Token.span

and arg = string option * expr

type stmt =
  | (* earlier cases *)
  | Set_member of {
      obj : string;
      field : string;
      value : expr;
      span : Token.span;
    }

type field = {
  fld_name : string;
  fld_ty : string;
  fld_var : bool;
}

type struct_decl = {
  sname : string;
  sfields : field list;
  sspan : Token.span;
}

type item =
  | (* earlier cases *)
  | IStruct of struct_decl
```

In a `Call`, `Some "x"` preserves the label in `Point(x: 1)`, while `None` represents the
positional argument in `add(1)`. `Member (base, "x", span)` can nest, so `line.b.x` becomes a
`Member` whose base is another `Member`. `Set_member` deliberately stores `obj` as a name rather
than an arbitrary expression because this first version accepts only one-level writes such as
`p.x = value`. A field keeps its written type name for Sema to resolve. Its `fld_var` Boolean is
`true` when the declaration begins with `var` and `false` when it begins with `let`; Sema uses it
to decide whether an assignment such as `p.x = 3` is allowed.

### The parser diagnostics added here

The parser reports the first missing piece at the token it found. These messages form part of the
concept's contract:

| source shape | message |
|---|---|
| `struct { }` | `expected a struct name` |
| `struct P var x: Int }` | `expected '{'` |
| `struct P { x: Int }` | `expected a stored property: 'var name: Type'` |
| `struct P { var : Int }` | `expected a property name` |
| `struct P { var x Int }` | `expected ':'` |
| `struct P { var x: }` | `expected a property type` |
| `struct P { var x: Int var y: Int }` | `expected newline or end of declaration` |
| end of input before the closing `}` | `expected '}'` |
| `p.` with no identifier after the dot | `expected a member name` |

`parse_struct` can produce all eight declaration errors above. Six come from its calls to
`parse_ident` and the given `expect` helper. It emits the stored-property and declaration-separator
messages directly. When it encounters an unexpected field introducer, it consumes that token and
continues looking for the next property or the closing brace.

### The diagnostics Sema owes you

You implement these checks in TODO(10d–f). Once they pass, lowering may assume every rule below has
already fired. Wording follows `swiftc
-typecheck` where the subset lets it (`swift/include/swift/AST/DiagnosticsSema.def`, line numbers
from the pinned snapshot); the differences are stated, not hidden.

| program | our message | swiftc |
|---|---|---|
| `Point(1, 2)` | `missing argument label 'x:' in call` (one per argument) | `missing argument labels 'x:y:' in call` — one message, plural (`missing_argument_labels`, l.1642) |
| `Point(z: 1, y: 2)` | `incorrect argument label in call (have 'z:', expected 'x:')` | `(have 'z:y:', expected 'x:y:')` — the whole label list (`wrong_argument_labels`, l.1646) |
| `Point(y: 2, x: 1)` | two `incorrect argument label` errors | `argument 'x' must precede argument 'y'` (`argument_out_of_order_named_named`, l.1651) |
| `Point(x: 1)` | `'Point' initializer expects 2 argument(s) but 1 given` | `missing argument for parameter 'y' in call` (`missing_argument_named`, l.1683) |
| `Point(x: "s", y: 2)` | `cannot convert value of type 'String' to specified type 'Int'` | `… to expected argument type 'Int'` (`cannot_convert_argument_value`, l.382) — we reuse 05's `check_expr` wording |
| `p.z`, where `p` is a `Point` with no field named `z` | `value of type 'Point' has no member 'z'` | **same** (`could_not_find_value_member`, l.70) |
| `n.x`, where `n` is an `Int` | `value of type 'Int' has no member 'x'` | **same** (`could_not_find_value_member`, l.70) |
| `let p …; p.x = 5` | `cannot assign to property: 'p' is a 'let' constant` | **same** (`assignment_lhs_is_immutable_property`, l.5379); swiftc points at the member, we at the statement |
| `struct S { let x: Int }; var s …; s.x = 2` | `cannot assign to property: 'x' is a 'let' constant` | **same** — a `let` field is immutable through every binding |
| `p == q` on structs | `binary operator '==' cannot be applied to two 'Point' operands` | **same** (`cannot_apply_binop_to_same_args`, l.220) — no `Equatable` until Exercise 3 |
| `let n: Int = p` | `cannot convert value of type 'Point' to specified type 'Int'` | **same** |
| `struct Box { var value: Missing }` | `cannot find type 'Missing' in scope` | **same** |
| `Nope(x: 1)` | `cannot find 'Nope' in scope` | **same** |
| `struct A {…}` twice | `invalid redeclaration of 'A'` | **same** (`invalid_redecl`, l.1110) |
| `print(p)` on a struct | `cannot print a value of type 'Point' (only Int, Double, Bool and String)` | **accepted** — swiftc prints `Point(x: 1, y: 2)` through reflection; ours has no runtime to do it, so sema refuses instead of letting IRGen crash |

Two more limitations of this concept: a **nested write** `l.b.x = 1` is
not parsed (`Set_member` is one level, `p.x = e`; swiftc accepts it — Exercise 1's `mutating`
machinery is the natural place to generalize), and `print` of a `Double` goes through C's `%g`
(`3` where swiftc prints `3.0`), which is why the oracle corpus keeps to `Int`/`Bool` fields.

## 3. Build it, step by step

Structs go through every stage, so the work is nine small holes, TODO(10a) to TODO(10i), in
pipeline order. Each has its own test file, read through a lab mode that stops right after its
stage, so do them in this order and watch each one go green:

| hole | file | you write | test file | lab mode |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10a | `token.ml`, `lexer.ml` | the `struct` keyword, `.` and `;` | `lexer-structs.t` | `--emit-tokens` |
| 10b | `parser.ml` | a `struct` declaration | `parser-struct-decls.t` | `--emit-ast` |
| 10c | `parser.ml` | `p.x`, `x:` labels, `p.x = e` | `parser-struct-uses.t` | `--emit-ast` |
| 10d | `sema.ml` | the struct registry | `sema-struct-decls.t` | `--typecheck` |
| 10e | `sema.ml` | the type of a field read | `sema-struct-exprs.t` | `--typecheck` |
| 10f | `sema.ml` | the checks on a field write | `sema-member-write.t` | `--typecheck` |
| 10g | `silgen.ml` | a field read → `struct_extract` | `silgen-member-read.t` | `--emit-sil` |
| 10h | `silgen.ml` | a field write → address + `store` | `silgen-member-write.t` | `--emit-sil` |
| 10i | `irgen.ml` | the three struct instructions | `irgen-structs.t` | `--emit-llvm`, `build` |

Given, so you do not write it: the new tree and SIL nodes (`ast.ml`, `tast.ml`, `sil.ml`); in Sema,
the check of `Point(x: 1, y: 2)` (`infer_initializer`: arity, labels, argument types) and the
refusal of `==` and `print` on a whole struct; in SILGen, the lowering of `Point(…)` to `struct`;
and in IRGen, the `%Point = type { i64, i64 }` declarations.

- **10a — `token.ml` + `lexer.ml`.** Add `struct` to `keyword_or_ident` in `token.ml`. In the
  lexer, a `.` is `Dot`, except that `..<` stays the one token it already is; and `;` becomes a
  `Newline` token, so the parser keeps a single statement separator.
- **10b — `parser.ml`.** Parse `struct Name { … }`: the stored properties in source order, each
  with its name, its written type, and whether it began with `var` or `let`. Newlines and `;` are
  the same token by now, and `skip_newlines parser` (given, beside `expect`) walks past a run of
  them.
- **10c — `parser.ml`, three places.** `parse_postfix` consumes any number of `.field` after an
  expression, nesting `Ast.Member`; the argument parser takes an optional `label:` (an `Ident`
  then a `Colon`) before each argument; and a statement of the form `name.field = expr` becomes an
  `Ast.Set_member`, recognised before the expression-statement fallback.
- **10d — `sema.ml`, the registry.** Two passes over the struct declarations: first register every
  name with an empty layout, so a field may name a struct declared later; then resolve each field's
  type and install the layout, fields in order. Record the `let` fields too: 10f needs them. A name
  declared twice is an error.
- **10e — `sema.ml`, a field read.** Infer the base; it must be a struct; find the field in its
  layout. The result is `Tast.Field (base, index, name)`, typed with the field's type: the index is
  what SILGen will use. An unknown field and a non-struct base are errors (§2 lists the messages).
  A base whose type is `TError` (already reported, concept 07) has every field: return `TError` and
  report nothing.
- **10f — `sema.ml`, a field write.** `p.x = e` needs `p` to be a `var` and `x` a `var` field, and
  `e` must check against the field's type. Record the field's index in `Tast.Set_member`. As in
  10e, a `TError` base reports nothing; check `e` against `TError`.
- **10g — `silgen.ml`, a field read.** You get `Tast.Field (operand, index, _)` and the field's
  type `ty`. Lower `operand` to a struct value and emit one `Sil.Struct_extract (value, index)` of
  type `ty`. There is nothing to look up: Sema already turned the name into `index`.
- **10h — `silgen.ml`, a field write.** You get `Set_member { obj; field = index; value }`. The
  variable's slot is in `builder.variables`; emit `Sil.Struct_element_addr (slot, index)`, typed
  with the field's type, then `Sil.Store` the value to that address. Whether you lower the value
  before or after taking the address does not matter; the tests accept both.
- **10i — `irgen.ml`, three instructions.** `Struct` is a chain of `insertvalue`, starting from
  `undef`, each step building on the previous register, the last being the complete value.
  `Struct_extract` is one `extractvalue`. `Struct_element_addr` is
  `getelementptr <struct type>, ptr <slot>, i32 0, i32 <index>`. `llvm_type (value_type value)`
  gives any value's LLVM type; `fresh_temp`, `lookup_operand` and `bind_operand` work as in 09.

Reference: `solution/` — after you have tried it.

## 4. Test it

```bash
make lab C=phase3-value-types/10-structs        # add T=sema-struct-exprs to run one file
```

Every `.t` file calls `./lab.exe`, built from **this directory's** library, so the report is about
your code here. One file per hole, in the order of §3, then the files that build and run:

| file | lab mode | green with | what it pins |
|---|---|---|---|
| `lexer-structs.t` | `--emit-tokens` | 10a | `struct` as a keyword, a lone `.`, the existing `..<`, and `;` |
| `parser-struct-decls.t` | `--emit-ast` | 10b | `var`/`let` stored properties in order with their written types, and the declaration errors of §2 |
| `parser-struct-uses.t` | `--emit-ast` | 10c | initializer labels, chained reads, one-level writes, a missing member name after `.` |
| `sema-struct-decls.t` | `--typecheck` | 10d | the two-pass registry, a field typed by a struct declared later, unknown types, duplicate names |
| `sema-struct-exprs.t` | `--typecheck` | 10e | member reads, first on function parameters, then on built structs; the initializer's label, arity and type errors (given code, run here because it needs your registry); the refusal of `==` and `print` on a whole struct |
| `sema-member-write.t` | `--typecheck` | 10f | a `let` binding, a `let` field, the assigned value's type |
| `silgen-member-read.t` | `--emit-sil` | 10g | `p.x` is a `load` then `struct_extract #0`; `p.y` is `#1`; a field of a fresh `Point(…)` or a call result needs no `load`; `l.b.x` is two extracts; a read inside a function |
| `silgen-member-write.t` | `--emit-sil` | 10h | `p.x = 9` is `struct_element_addr #0` of p's slot, then `store`; two writes to one slot; after `var q = p`, a write addresses **q's** slot; a write in a loop |
| `irgen-structs.t` | `--emit-llvm`, `build` | 10i | the named type, the `insertvalue` chain, `extractvalue`, `getelementptr`; then programs **run**: 3/4, the value-semantics `1`/`99`, a struct argument and result, writes in a loop, a `Double` field |
| `oracle.t` | `build`, `--typecheck` | all | **the headline**: below |

`oracle.t` has two halves. The first builds the 16 programs of `oracle-corpus.txt` with
`swiftc -Onone` and with `./lab.exe build`, runs both, and requires the same output and exit code.
The second asks both compilers for a verdict on the 20 programs of `typecheck-corpus.txt`, six
that swiftc accepts and fourteen it rejects, and requires the same verdict. The second half needs
only the front-end holes, 10a–10f.

Two suites run in-process. `test_structs.ml` (`structs`) has one group per test file above, named
after it; its lexer and parser groups stop before Sema, so early holes can pass while later ones
are unwritten. `test_exercises.ml` (`exercises-10`) holds the three optional §6 exercises, each
group skipping itself until it sees that exercise started.

### Two things worth knowing before you read a red report

**The lowering tests compare relationships, not names.** They check which slot an address comes
from and which value is stored, not the spelling of `%6` or `%t3`, and they accept either order
for two independent instructions, such as generating the stored value before or after the field
address. Those choices do not change what the SIL or LLVM means.

**A hole can read `FAIL` before you touch it.** Several holes in the skeleton fall back to the old
behaviour instead of stopping at a `TODO`: until 10a, `struct` lexes as a plain identifier, so a
program declaring a struct produces wrong output rather than reaching a `TODO`, and the report
prints the differences. Fill the holes in order and read only the first red file.

## 5. Benchmark it

This benchmark passes and returns a six-field struct 50 million times:

```swift
struct Six {
  var a: Int
  var b: Int
  var c: Int
  var d: Int
  var e: Int
  var f: Int
}

func rotateAndAdd(_ value: Six, _ step: Int) -> Six {
  let first = value.b + step % 7
  return Six(a: first, b: value.c, c: value.d, d: value.e, e: value.f, f: value.a)
}

var value = Six(a: 1, b: 2, c: 3, d: 4, e: 5, f: 6)
for step in 0 ..< 50000000 {
  value = rotateAndAdd(value, step)
}
print(value.a + value.b + value.c + value.d + value.e + value.f)
```

Run all four variants with:

```bash
make bench C=phase3-value-types/10-structs
```

The runner first checks that their stdout is byte-identical. It then reports the best of five
runs after one warm-up. On this machine:

```text
Struct value benchmark -- 50,000,000 six-field updates
  compiling and checking four binaries... done
  output: 150000018 (all four binaries agree)
  native runtime, best of 5 after one warm-up:
    swiftml (clang default)     0.216 s
    swiftml + clang -O2         0.023 s
    swiftc -Onone               3.609 s
    swiftc -O                   0.024 s
  clang -O2 speedup: 9.17x
  swiftc -O speedup: 150.15x
  optimized gap: 0.98x (swiftml / swiftc)
```

`swiftc -Onone` disables optimization for a predictable debugging build. `swiftc -O` enables
Swift's SIL optimizer and LLVM's speed optimizations. `clang` without an optimization flag leaves
our generated LLVM at `-O0`; `clang -O2` runs LLVM's standard optimization pipeline.

This program is friendly to LLVM: inlining and scalar replacement remove the temporary aggregate
copies, so our direct SIL-to-LLVM translation reaches the same speed as `swiftc -O` here. That does
not make the SIL optimizer redundant. With later Swift features, SIL still has ownership, generic,
and reference-counting information that a basic LLVM translation has already erased, and its
high-level optimizations can produce code LLVM alone cannot recover. Timings vary by machine.

## 6. Exercises

These are optional. `make exercises C=phase3-value-types/10-structs` runs only their
self-detecting suite. They also appear in `make lab` as `TODO (optional)` until you start one.

1. **Methods + `mutating`.** Lower `struct Point { … func dist() -> Int { … } }` to a function with an
   implicit `self` parameter (read-only); a `mutating func` takes `self` by **address**
   (`struct_element_addr` territory) so it can write fields. This is how Swift threads `self`.
2. **Computed properties.** `var area: Int { return w * h }` — a property with a getter, lowered to a
   call, not a stored field. Distinguish stored vs. computed in the layout.
3. **`Equatable`.** Let `struct Pair: Equatable { … }` use `==` and `!=`, by synthesizing `==`
   from the fields, compared pairwise — a first taste of Swift's protocol-conformance synthesis
   (full protocols are Phase 5, concept 21). As in swiftc, a struct that does not declare
   `: Equatable` still has no `==`, and every stored property must be `Equatable` itself.

The answer key is `solution/exercises/`; `make check-exercises C=phase3-value-types/10-structs`
builds it and runs both the exercise tests and this concept's own suite with it.

## 7. Recap & what's next

You added `struct` — a whole new **type kind** — through every stage, and made **value semantics**
real: structs are aggregates copied on assignment, with reads via `struct_extract` (a value) and
writes via `struct_element_addr` (an address into the variable's own slot). Programs run and match
swiftc.

Next, **11-enums-adts**: `enum` with associated values — **tagged unions**, the other half of
algebraic data types. Where a struct is "all of these fields at once" (a product), an enum is "exactly
one of these cases" (a sum), laid out as a **tag + payload**. Then **12-pattern-matching** gives you
`switch` to take them apart — and **13-optionals** reveals that `Optional` was just an enum all along.

## 8. Appendix — solution

The complete files are in `solution/`. These are the new cases, in pipeline order:

```ocaml
(* token.ml + lexer.ml *)
| "struct" -> Kw_struct

| '.' ->
    ignore (advance_char lexer);
    if peek_char lexer = '.' && peek_next_char lexer = '<' then (
      ignore (advance_char lexer); ignore (advance_char lexer);
      make_token start_position lexer Token.DotDotLt)
    else make_token start_position lexer Token.Dot
| ';' -> ignore (advance_char lexer); make_token start_position lexer Token.Newline
```

```ocaml
(* parser.ml — postfix reads and optional argument labels *)
and parse_postfix parser expression =
  if peek_kind parser = Token.Dot then (
    ignore (advance parser);
    match peek_kind parser with
    | Token.Ident field_name ->
        let field_token = advance parser in
        parse_postfix parser
          (Ast.Member (expression, field_name,
             span_between (Ast.expr_span expression) field_token.Token.span))
    | _ ->
        Diagnostics.error parser.diagnostics (peek parser).Token.span
          "expected a member name";
        expression)
  else expression

let label =
  match peek_kind parser with
  | Token.Ident name when peek_kind_at parser 1 = Token.Colon ->
      ignore (advance parser); ignore (advance parser); Some name
  | _ -> None
```

`parse_struct` follows the grammar directly: consume the keyword, name, and `{`; skip separators;
for every `var` or `let`, parse `name : Type`, append an `Ast.field`, and stop at `}`. The member-write
arm uses the four-token lookahead from §2 and constructs `Ast.Set_member` before the expression
fallback.

```ocaml
(* sema.ml — the registry is deliberately two-pass *)
List.iter (function
  | Ast.IStruct struct_decl ->
      if Hashtbl.mem struct_layouts struct_decl.Ast.sname then
        report_error struct_decl.Ast.sspan
          (Printf.sprintf "invalid redeclaration of '%s'" struct_decl.Ast.sname);
      Hashtbl.replace struct_layouts struct_decl.Ast.sname
        { Types.sl_name = struct_decl.Ast.sname; sl_fields = [] }
  | _ -> ()) program.Ast.items;

List.iter (function
  | Ast.IStruct struct_decl ->
      let fields = List.map (fun (field : Ast.field) ->
        (field.Ast.fld_name,
         resolve_type struct_decl.Ast.sspan field.Ast.fld_ty)) struct_decl.Ast.sfields in
      List.iter (fun (field : Ast.field) ->
        if not field.Ast.fld_var then
          Hashtbl.replace immutable_fields
            (struct_decl.Ast.sname, field.Ast.fld_name) ()) struct_decl.Ast.sfields;
      Hashtbl.replace struct_layouts struct_decl.Ast.sname
        { Types.sl_name = struct_decl.Ast.sname; sl_fields = fields }
  | _ -> ()) program.Ast.items
```

Member reads look up `field_type` after `infer_expression` returns `TStruct name`. Initializers compare the
argument list with `sl_fields` in order. Member writes use the binding's `is_var` bit and the
`immutable_fields` table before calling `check_expr value field_type`; the complete diagnostic branches are
in `solution/sema.ml`.

```ocaml
(* SILGen — member read is a value; member write is an address. Sema supplied the INDEX,
   so neither arm looks anything up. *)
  (* read a field out of a struct VALUE with struct_extract. The INDEX came from Sema, so
     there is no layout to look up and no name to match — and no way to disagree about
     either. *)
  | Tast.Field (operand_expression, index, _) ->
      let struct_value = gen_expr builder operand_expression in
      emit builder (Sil.Struct_extract (struct_value, index)) ty

  | Tast.Set_member { obj = object_name; field = index; value; _ } ->
      (* `p.x = expression`: take the field's ADDRESS in p's slot, then store — this is
         what makes a struct a value type, since p has its own slot distinct from any copy.
         The index is Sema's; SILGen looks nothing up. *)
      let stored = gen_expr builder value in
      let object_address = Hashtbl.find builder.variables object_name in
      let field_address =
        emit builder
          (Sil.Struct_element_addr (object_address, index))
          (value_type builder stored)
      in
      emit_void builder (Sil.Store (stored, field_address))
```

```ocaml
(* IRGen — aggregates in LLVM *)
| Sil.Struct fields ->
    let struct_type = llvm_type (value_type value) in
    let aggregate_operand = ref "undef" in
    List.iteri (fun field_index field_value ->
      let result_operand = fresh_temp () in
      emit (Printf.sprintf "  %s = insertvalue %s %s, %s %s, %d\n"
           result_operand struct_type !aggregate_operand
           (llvm_type (value_type field_value))
           (lookup_operand field_value) field_index);
      aggregate_operand := result_operand) fields;
    bind_operand value !aggregate_operand
| Sil.Struct_extract (aggregate, field_index) ->
    let result_operand = fresh_temp () in
    emit (Printf.sprintf "  %s = extractvalue %s %s, %d\n"
         result_operand (llvm_type (value_type aggregate))
         (lookup_operand aggregate) field_index);
    bind_operand value result_operand
| Sil.Struct_element_addr (address, field_index) ->
    let result_operand = fresh_temp () in
    emit (Printf.sprintf "  %s = getelementptr %s, ptr %s, i32 0, i32 %d\n"
         result_operand (llvm_type (value_type address))
         (lookup_operand address) field_index);
    bind_operand value result_operand
```

## 9. Exercise solutions

The answer key, `solution/exercises/`, applies all three, and every difference from the stock key
is marked `EX1`, `EX2` or `EX3`. All three are lowered in Sema, to the functions the compiler
already knows how to lower: a method is an ordinary function with `self` as its first parameter.
So SILGen and IRGen learn only one new thing, passing an argument by address (exercise 1).

### 1 — methods and `mutating`

The parser accepts `func` and `mutating func` in a struct body, and `recv.m(args)` after an
expression (`Ast.Method_call`). Sema turns a method `m` of `S` into the function `S.m`, with `self`
first:

```swift
struct Counter {
  var value: Int
  func read() -> Int { return self.value }
  mutating func increment() { self.value = self.value + 1 }
}
```

becomes the functions `Counter.read(self)` and `Counter.increment(self)`, and `counter.read()` is
the call `Counter.read(counter)`. Inside a method, a bare property or method name means
`self.name`, so `value = value + 1` works too.

A non-`mutating` method takes `self` by value, a copy, and Sema binds it as a `let`: writing
`self.value` there is refused, with swiftc's "cannot assign to property: 'self' is immutable". A
`mutating` method must change the caller's variable, so it takes `self` by **address**: the call
passes the receiver's slot (`Tast.Address_of`), and inside the method `self` *is* that slot, with
no copy of its own. The SIL shows it, with swiftc's `$*` spelling for an address type:

```
sil @Counter.increment(%0 : $*Counter) -> $() {
bb0:
  %1 = load %0 $Counter               // read through the caller's slot
  %2 = struct_extract %1, #0 $Int
  %3 = integer_literal $Int, 1
  %4 = binop "+" %2, %3 $Int
  %5 = struct_element_addr %0, #0     // and write back into it
  store %4 to %5
  return
}
```

The receiver must be storage that can change: a `var`, or a path of `var` fields inside one
(`line.end.bump()` passes the address of `end` inside `line`'s slot). A `let`, a `let` field or a
call result is refused with swiftc's wording, e.g. "cannot use mutating member on immutable value:
'box' is a 'let' constant". In LLVM the address parameter is a `ptr`, and since an argument's SIL
type is that of what it points at, IRGen takes each call's argument types from the callee's
signature.

Why not copy `self` back after the call instead? That works only for a `mutating` method that
returns nothing. `print(counter.bump())`, with `bump` both changing `self` and returning a value,
needs two results from one call, and the address gives them for free. swiftc passes `self` by
address for the same reason (an `@inout` parameter).

### 2 — computed properties

`var area: Int { return width * height }` in a struct body is parsed as a computed property. It
has no storage, so the layout keeps only the stored fields (`%Rectangle = type { i64, i64 }`).
Sema makes its body a getter, the function `Rectangle.area(self)`, and a read `r.area` that finds
no stored field named `area` becomes a call to it. Stored and computed properties read the same at
the use site, which is the point: uniform access. Assigning to one is refused, "cannot assign to
property: 'area' is a get-only property".

### 3 — `Equatable`

`struct Pair: Equatable { var first: Int; var second: Bool }` is parsed with its conformance list.
Sema checks that every stored property is `Equatable` (the scalar types, or a struct that declared
it), else "type 'Pair' does not conform to protocol 'Equatable'". The first `a == b` on a `Pair`
synthesizes the function `Pair.__eq(a, b)`, the `&&` of the fields' comparisons, so it stops at
the first field that differs; a struct field compares through its own `__eq`. `a == b` is a call
to it, and `a != b` compares that call with `false`. Without `: Equatable`, `==` on a struct is
still the error it was. One gap remains, and it is this concept's, not the exercise's: comparing
two `String`s is not lowered by this back end, so neither is a `String` field.
